Phase 2: Strength & Neuromuscular Control

At the transition from phase 1 to phase 2, it is expected that pain and swelling have settled down and adequate knee range of motion (ROM) has been established. The focus of the rehab can now grow to include building strength and greater neuromuscular control. Key outcomes from Phase 1 will continue to be monitored, including swelling and ROM assessments which remain a part of the criteria. Progressions in both exercise complexity and loading parameters will occur continuously throughout this phase, and it is important that the practitioner monitors these progressions and the athlete’s responses carefully. The progressions made in this phase will set the athlete up for more dynamic exercises in Phase 3.

ImportantMost Important Goals — Phase 1
  • Rebuild muscular strength, especially the quadriceps and hamstrings
  • Re-establish neuromuscular control (stability, balance, )
  • Listen to the body: be aware of pain, swelling or ROM regressions and adjust training accordingly

Outcomes generally reflect maintaining a healthy knee, increased lower body muscular endurance and strength, and improved static postural stability. Frank Reynolds’s progress towards these goals will be assessed via the criteria seen below. Detailed description of each criteria and the associated testing methodology can be found in the Testing section.

Phase 2 Criteria
Outcome Measure Goal Score
Passive Knee Extension ≤ 0° 0
Passive Knee Flexion ≥ 125° 127
Swelling ≤ 0 0
Ankle Dorsiflexion ≥ 10cm 11
Single Leg Bridge ≥ 20 Reps 20
Single Leg Calf Raises ≥ 20 20
Side Bridge ≥ 30s 30
Single Leg Rise ≥ 10 10
TrapBar Deadlift ≥ 110 kg 110
Quad Strength > 75% 87
Hamstring Strength > 75% 82
Single Leg Balance (Eyes Open) ≥ 45s 45
Single Leg Balance (Eyes Closed) ≥ 9s 9
Y-Balance ≥ 75% 92
Goals met: 14/14 100%

What does the research say?

Knee Health

By satisfying phase 1 criteria before beginning phase 2, we can be confident that the knee is prepared for the increases in load required to build muscular strength. An abundance of pain and swelling at this stage will negatively affect joint proprioception [1] and limit neuromuscular activation via the process of arthrogenic muscle inhibition (AMI) [2].

Development of Muscular Strength

Perhaps the number one priority during this phase is to restore muscular strength, particularly in the knee extensor muscles [3]. At this stage of the rehab, deficits in quadriceps muscle volume, activation and strength resulting from injury and surgery will be persistent [4]. In response to these deficits, athletes will use inter- and intra-limb compensations to reduce the knee extensor moment, and efforts must be made to directly target the quadriceps in order to produce desired adaptations in strength and hypertrophy [5]. The consensus across studies is that a limb symmetry index of 80% should be achieved by the end of Phase 2 (mid-phase) rehab [6] . Additionally, although absolute strength values will differ among individuals, it is important to track raw strength numbers for each limb, to ensure that knee function is not being over-estimated by symmetry values alone [ ]. If testing on an isokinetic machine, peak torque at 90º/s should be > 2 Nm/kg [3]. Determination of CSI Pacific recommended values for peak force using the Tindeq is a work in progress.

It is also common to see persistent hamstring strength deficits for extended periods of time following ACLR [7]. The hamstrings serve as a critical dynamic stabilizer of the knee following ACLR, with their co-contraction acting to reduce anterior tibial translation and reduce direct load on the reconstructed graft which is especially important in early and mid-phase rehabilitation when quadriceps function is likely compromised [8]. Highlighting the importance of strengthening the hamstring muscles, one study demonstrated over 10x greater risk of ACL re-injury after ACLR for every 10% decrease in knee flexor to extensor strength ratio in professional football players [9]. Hamstring strengthening should involve a “holistic approach” which incorporates both knee and hip dominant exercises [10].

In addition to knee extensor and flexor strength, other muscle groups both proximal and distal to the knee will play key roles following ACLR. Muscles of the ankle and lower leg act as agonists to the ACL, helping to prevent anterior tibial translation [11] and generate large forces during tasks such as running [12] and landing [13]. This means strong lower leg muscles will help protect the knee joint during more intense activities later in rehab. Deficits in lumbo-pelvic-hip muscle strength are also common following ACLR [14]. The hip abductors and external rotators (e.g. the gluteal muscles) are important for preventing dynamic knee valgus in loaded CKC exercises that will be performed throughout the rest of the rehab [15,16]. Direct evidence on the importance of hip adductor strengthening is limited at this time, however evidence from knee pathology research demonstrates that adductor strengthening significantly improves knee pain, physical function, and lower limb strength, supporting its inclusion as part of a comprehensive kinetic chain approach to knee rehabilitation [17].

Now that the importance of developing/re-building lower limb muscle strength has been established, the research can inform HOW this will be accomplished. One model of mid-phase rehabilitation proposes two blocks which allow specific programming based on the functional status of the athlete [3]. The first block involves non-weight-bearing isolated exercises performed at lower intensities. This includes both OKC (e.g. leg extension) and CKC (e.g. leg press) exercises The second block would involve an increased proportion of functional exercise (e.g. squats, lunges, hinges) with all exercises performed at higher intensities. Overall, the CSI Pacific Phase 2 rehab programs agree with these principles, however they are structured along a continuum as opposed to separate blocks. Strength training will progress from isolated to functional and from low load to high load. Volume may start in a middle range (to prioritize movement quality over intensity, increase as the body begins to adapt to these movement with the goal of increasing metabolic stress to target muscular strength and hypertrophy, and then volume will begin to decrease as the athlete becomes capable of lifting heavier loads. The training program may include both low/no-load full ROM leg extension as well as ROM-restricted leg extension when the patient is able to lift heavier loads. Minimal ACL strain and reduced PFJ reaction forces have been observed during quadriceps contractions performed between 45-90º of knee flexion, and therefore this is the recommended ROM for loading to be introduced [18]. Early introduction of isometrics is recommended if tolerated well by the athlete, beginning with isometric leg extension performed at a fixed angle between 90-60º (5x45s, 1-2x per day). Full ROM (90-0º) against gravity/low loads can be performed once able to comfortably achieve 90º knee flexion. Restricted ROM loaded knee extensions may begin 4 weeks post ACLR (Tempo 3:03, 15-25RM loads).

Neuromuscular Control and Movement Quality

Altered movement quality is well documented following ACLR [19] and is associated with increased risk of secondary injury [20] and early onset osteoarthritis [21]. As discussed in Phase 1, there are many factors contributing to movement quality deficits following ACLR including the loss or damage of mechanoreceptors which typically provide somatosensory information to the brain about joint position and movement, a.k.a. proprioception [22]. Altered movement quality at this stage may also be observed in reduced static postural stability [23] and reduced dorsi-flexor ROM [24].

Targeted movement interventions found in the ACL Rehab Programs are based on motor learning principles, specifically applied to movement re-training post-ACLR [25]. Motor learning is defined as an individual’s ability to acquire motor skills with a sustained change in performance as a function of practice or experience [26], and thus the program will involve the repeated practice of important skills. It is important that prior to adding load or velocity to any movement that optimal technique is demonstrated, and therefore task progression will be based on both movement complexity and load [3]. At the start of phase 2, emphasis and attention to detail on movement technique will be high, and loading will be relatively low. Direct loading of the knee joint and affected tissues will be carefully progressed. For the practitioner, the ability to assess and coach movement quality in real-time is crucial. This can additionally be aided by video analysis allowing bio-feedback and improved cognitive understanding for the athlete. Further review of motor learning approaches following ACLR is recommended [25] in order to maximize the effectiveness of the Phase 1 training programs for realizing improvements in movement quality.

Testing

Each card below contains a detailed description of the tests to be conducted during this phase of rehab.

Passive Knee Extension

Measured in Supine with a long arm goniometer

  • Bony Landmarks: greater trochanter, lateral femoral condyle, lateral malleolus

Criteria: ≤ 0°

Passive Knee Flexion

Measured in Supine with a long arm goniometer

  • Bony Landmarks: greater trochanter, lateral femoral condyle, lateral malleolus

Criteria: ≥ 125°

Swelling

Stroke test [27]

  • Zero: No wave produced on downstroke
    Trace: Small wave on medial side with downstroke
    1+: Large bulge on medial side with downstroke
    2+: Effusion spontaneously returns to medial side after upstroke
    3+: So much fluid that it is not possible to move the effusion out of the medial aspect of the knee

Criteria: ≤ 0

Ankle Dorsiflexion

Knee to Wall Test

  • Injured side dorsiflexion should be > 10cm and > 90% of un-injured side.

Criteria: ≥ 10cm

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Max

Single Leg Bridge

﻿Subjects lie supine on the floor with one heel on a 60cm (~24”) high box. The knee of the test leg is slightly bent at 20° and opposite leg is bent to 90° hip and knee flexion with their arms crossed over chest. Subjects elevate the hips as high as possible and the assessor places a target at this height. Repeat this action as many times as possible touching the target each time. The test concludes when the subject is unable to bridge to the target [freckleton2013?].

  • Input the number of reps completed. The goal is >20 reps and injured leg reps >85% of un-injured leg.

Criteria: ≥ 20 Reps

Single Leg Calf Raises

﻿Subjects stand on one foot on the edge of a step and performs a calf raise through full range of motion. Calf raises are performed at 1 repetition every 2 seconds. The test concludes when subjects are unable to move through full range or slow below the cadence outlined above (Hebert et al, 2017).

  • Input the number of reps completed. The goal is >20 reps and injured leg reps >85% of un-injured leg.

Criteria: ≥ 20

Side Bridge

﻿Subjects lie on an exercise mat on their side with legs extended. The top foot is placed in front on the lower foot, then subjects lift their hips off the mat to maintain a straight line over their full body length for as long as able. The test ends when the hips return to the mat (McGill et al, 1999).

  • Input the amount of time the position is held. The goal is >30 seconds and injured side tima >85% of un-injured side.

Criteria: ≥ 30s

Single Leg Rise

﻿Subjects sit on a box with the test heel 10cm from the edge of the box and the box height set so that the test leg is bent to 90deg. With hands folded across the chest, the subject aims to stand up from the sitting position, and sit down as many times as possible (Culvenor et al., 2016 & Thorstensson et al., 2004).

  • Input the number of reps completed. The goal is >10 reps and injured leg reps >85% of un-injured leg.

Criteria: ≥ 10

TrapBar Deadlift

Set up the TrapBar on a lifting platform, using blocks as needed so that the subject’s knees are flexed to 90 degrees when placing tension on the bar without lifting it. Progressively perform single repetitions until a 1RM is established.

  • Record the maximum load in kg. The target load for graduation from this phase is 1.5x BM. This criteria may vary based on initial training status pre-injury.

Criteria: ≥ 110 kg

Repetitions: 1

Calculation: Max

Quad Strength

Isometric Strength at 90°

  • Seated with hip and knees flexed at 90°. Dynamometer placed on the anterior aspect of the shank, proximal to the ankle joint. Target score to complete this phase is 75% LSI compared to un-injured leg.

Criteria: > 75%

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Max

Hamstring Strength

Isometric Strength at 90°

  • Seated with hip and knees flexed at 90°. Dynamometer placed on the anterior aspect of the shank, proximal to the ankle joint. Target score to complete this phase is 75% LSI compared to un-injured leg.

Criteria: > 75%

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Max

Single Leg Balance (Eyes Open)

﻿Subjects stand on one leg with other leg raised and arms crossed over the chest. The assessor uses a stopwatch to time how long stance is maintained with eyes open (Springer et al, 2007).

  • Time ends when; • Arms are uncrossed • Opposite foot touches the floor • Movement of the stance foot • 45 secs has elapsed (maximum time)

Criteria: ≥ 45s

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Max

Single Leg Balance (Eyes Closed)

﻿Subjects stand on one leg with other leg raised and arms crossed over the chest. The assessor uses a stopwatch to time how long stance is maintained with eyes closed (Springer et al, 2007).

  • Time ends when; • Arms are uncrossed • Opposite foot touches the floor • Movement of the stance foot • 9 secs has elapsed (maximum time) • Eyes are opened

Criteria: ≥ 9s

Repetitions: 2

Calculation: Max

Y-Balance

Composite Score

  • The composite score combines Anterior, Postero-Medial and Postero-Lateral. Our current calculation places equal weight on each score. The displayed score represents the average score on the injured limb as a percentage of the average score on the non-injured limb. placing equal weight on each score. Currently we are not multiplying by limb length so this is not necessarily comparable between athletes. Composite score will be used for Phase Criteria, while individual Y-Balance scores can be found in the more detialed Phase Progress reports.

Criteria: ≥ 75%

Repetitions: 3 Each

Calculation: A+PL+PM/3*100

The Program

Below you will find links to your training programs.

Phase 2: Program 1

Figure 1 shows an example weekly schedule for this phase of the rehabilitation. The schedule is built around 3x per week targeted strength sessions with 48 hours of recovery between sessions. Non-ACLR workouts on Tuesday and Thursday target strength and neuromuscular control in the rest of the body (e.g. contralateral limb, upper body, core) and are accompanied by targeted BFR work for the affected limb. Twice weekly pool sessions are key at this stage for improving movement patterns in a de-loaded environment. Cardiovascular fitness is trained twice per week, a volume and frequency sufficient to develop and maintain these qualities while prioritizing the primary targets of Phase 2 rehab (e.g. quadriceps strength).

Here are some descriptions of what you can expect throughout these programs

  • Progression of exercises during this phase will be dependent on reactive pain, swelling, and ROM changes, all of which are normal and expected at this stage. It is unlikely that the athlete’s progression will align perfectly with the program; expect to make changes and be ready to picot on a daily basis

  • Development of muscular strength: Emphasis will progress as follows:

    • Non-weight Bearing –> Weight Bearing

    • Machine-Based -> Functional

    • Lower Intensity (12-20 RM) –> Moderate Intensity (8-12 RM)

    • Volume will first increase to increase proximity to maximum intensity at light loads, then decrease as loads begin to increase

  • Both OKC and CKC exercises will be prescribed throughout this phase

    • Isometric leg extension performed at a fixed angle between 90-60º (5x45s, 1-2x per day)

    • Restricted ROM (45-90º) loaded leg extensions may begin 4 weeks post ACLR (15-25RM loads)

  • Direct loading of the patellofemoral joint will start LOW and progress as tolerated

Additional Resources

Whole Body Fitness

At the same time that rehab is progressing to include more strength and neuromuscular training for the knee, the rest of the body should also be on track to begin the training needed to restore full-body neuromuscular and physiological function. It is important that an athlete commences later phases of rehabilitation with sufficient physical fitness to allow for intense training needed to return to high level of athletic performance. Evidence suggests that cardiovascular fitness in athletes can remain below pre-injury levels for long periods of time following ACLR [28]. Given the time-frames required to develop these capacities, it is important that they are addressed as early as possible, as opposed to waiting until later stages of the rehab where they may find themselves lacking the fitness required to reach high intensities of training. Upper body strength is also a key component of whole body fitness, and can be trained effectively even when the athlete is still in a non- or low-load-bearing stage (e.g. pull-ups, bench-press, seated shoulder press, seated rows). Lumbo-pelvic-hip (a.k.a. core) strengthening can also continue to progress during this phase, assuming the athlete has met straight-leg-raise quadriceps activation criteria, and given exercises that place little stress on the PFJ.

With all that said, it is important to distinguish between must-haves and nice-to-haves and to prioritize training accordingly. For example, development of cardiovascular fitness is important however in comparison to something like knee extensor strength, it does not prevent the athlete from progressing the complexity and intensity of rehab exercises during this phase [3]. On the contrary, pushing too hard on the stationary bike, for example, may lead to reactive pain,swelling, and fatigue that can delay the attainment of other more pertinent qualities. Therefore, periodization during this phase will prioritize direct rehabilitation of the knee while including thoughtful and reasonable programming to target whole body fitness.

Blood Flow Restriction

BFR may continue to be a useful tool for building muscular strength and hypertrophy during the transition from Phase 1 to 2.

Another more recent study did not report how early BFR began after surgery, but did use the following criteria to begin BFR: able to stand on one leg unsupported for >5s, knee ROM between 0-90º, able to perform SLR with sufficient quadriceps activation [29] . Patients performed the traditional 30-15-15-15 reps of leg press
